description: This policy brief examines AI-generated video in the U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict through the concepts of narrative occupancy, machine addressability, and machine audience. It argues that synthetic wartime media should not be assessed only by whether it persuades or deceives human audiences. As search systems, retrieval pipelines, large language models, and AI agents increasingly mediate digital information, synthetic content may remain discoverable and retrievable beyond its period of direct human attention. The brief analyzes three illustrative cases: Iranian state-linked synthetic mobilization, President Donald Trump’s Kharg Island post as synthetic battlefield representation, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s AI-generated campaign video as relational fabrication. It concludes that the central policy challenge is not only detecting synthetic media, but preserving distinctions among what occurred, what was claimed, what was depicted, and what was generated across machine-mediated information systems.
abstract: AI-generated video in the U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict should be assessed not only by its ability to persuade or deceive human audiences. As search systems, retrieval pipelines, large language models, and AI agents increasingly mediate digital information, synthetic content may remain retrievable beyond its period of direct human attention. This policy brief introduces narrative occupancy, the persistent representation of a claim or association across machine-accessible information objects, and machine addressability, the degree to which such information can be discovered, parsed, and retrieved by automated systems. Together, these concepts extend information-warfare analysis from human attention toward machine-mediated information competition. The brief analyzes three illustrative cases: Iranian state-linked synthetic mobilization, President Donald Trump’s Kharg Island post as synthetic battlefield representation, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s AI-generated campaign video as relational fabrication. It emphasizes that machine accessibility should not be confused with retrieval, acceptance, influence, or proof of agent-directed intent. The policy problem extends beyond deepfake detection: machine-mediated systems must preserve distinctions among an event, a depiction, an allegation, a denial, and independently verified evidence.

methodology.framework_name: Narrative Occupancy, Machine Addressability, and Machine Audience Framework
methodology.source_basis: Exploratory, mechanism-oriented policy assessment based on publicly available reporting, research literature on deepfakes and synthetic media, AI-agent and crawler analysis, C2PA provenance specifications, Cloudflare automated traffic analysis, CSIS and Brookings conflict-information analysis, and EPINOVA MCCM-related conflict-monitoring work.
methodology.case_context: AI-generated political and wartime video in the U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict, with three illustrative cases: Iranian state-linked synthetic mobilization, Trump’s Kharg Island post, and Netanyahu’s AI-generated campaign video.
methodology.core_problem: The central analytical problem is whether synthetic wartime claims can remain machine-accessible after direct human attention declines, and whether automated systems preserve evidentiary status when retrieving, summarizing, and re-presenting contested information.
central_claims: AI-generated wartime video should be assessed not only by human persuasion or deception, but also by machine-mediated persistence and retrieval.
Narrative occupancy describes persistent representation of a claim, interpretation, or actor relationship across machine-accessible information objects over time.
Machine addressability describes discoverability, parsability, and retrievability by automated systems, not proof of acceptance, influence, or downstream action.
Machine audience is analytical shorthand for heterogeneous non-human systems, including crawlers, search indexes, retrieval systems, language models, recommendation systems, and AI agents.
Synthetic political representation can compress grievances, visualize unverified battlefield outcomes, or fabricate relationships even when not accepted as authentic evidence.
The central integrity challenge is preservation of distinctions among event, claim, depiction, simulation, allegation, denial, correction, and verification.

The evidence does not justify adding a new quantified MCCM indicator; synthetic-content production should be tracked as an input to existing narrative-amplification and information-distortion mechanisms.

analytical_lenses.name: Narrative Occupancy
analytical_lenses.description: Tracks persistence of claims, interpretations, or actor relationships across machine-accessible information objects over time.

analytical_lenses.name: Machine Addressability
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses whether information can be discovered, parsed, and retrieved by automated systems while distinguishing accessibility from influence.

analytical_lenses.name: Machine Audience
analytical_lenses.description: Treats crawlers, search systems, retrieval tools, language models, recommendation systems, and agents as heterogeneous intermediaries of political information.

analytical_lenses.name: Synthetic Political Representation
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses how generative media visually constructs events, relationships, coalitions, or imagined outcomes.

analytical_lenses.name: Epistemic Status Preservation
analytical_lenses.description: Evaluates whether systems preserve distinctions among what occurred, what was claimed, what was depicted, and what was verified.

analytical_lenses.name: MCCM Monitoring Integration
analytical_lenses.description: Treats synthetic-content observations as provenance-rich inputs to narrative warfare monitoring without prematurely creating a new quantified indicator.

dimensions.name: Narrative Occupancy
dimensions.description: Persistent representation of a specific claim, interpretation, or actor relationship across machine-accessible information objects over time.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Synthetic artifacts can generate derivative reporting, screenshots, transcripts, commentary, fact-checks, and machine-generated summaries.
dimensions.interpretation: Occupancy is not persuasion, dominance, or propaganda success.

dimensions.name: Temporal Persistence
dimensions.description: Whether the proposition remains retrievable across multiple observation points.
dimensions.interpretation: Persistence should be measured separately from engagement.

dimensions.name: Source Lineage
dimensions.description: Distinguishes independent sources from derivative reporting, reposts, or summaries originating from the same artifact.
dimensions.interpretation: Repeated references may not equal independent corroboration.

dimensions.name: Stance and Epistemic Status
dimensions.description: Distinguishes assertion, quotation, denial, satire, correction, verification, depiction, and simulation.
dimensions.interpretation: Entity co-occurrence should not be treated as occupancy of the same claim.

dimensions.name: Machine Addressability
dimensions.description: Degree to which an information object can be discovered, parsed, and retrieved by automated systems.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Crawling and indexing create machine accessibility but do not prove retrieval, acceptance, model incorporation, influence, or action.
dimensions.interpretation: Addressability is descriptive rather than optimization-oriented.

dimensions.name: Machine Audience
dimensions.description: Non-human systems that serve as intermediate consumers and processors of political information.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Includes crawlers, search indexes, recommendation systems, retrieval-augmented generation systems, language models, and AI agents.
dimensions.interpretation: Machine audience is heterogeneous and should not be treated as a single interpreting subject.

dimensions.name: Epistemic Compression
dimensions.description: Loss of distinctions among event, claim, depiction, simulation, allegation, denial, and verification during repeated representation or summarization.
dimensions.observed_pattern: A qualified report about an AI-generated depiction may be summarized later as though the depicted event occurred.
dimensions.interpretation: Qualification, provenance, negation, and source dependence are substantive information.

dimensions.name: Synthetic Mobilization
dimensions.description: Use of generative media to compress grievances, identities, histories, and political targets into a mobilizing frame.
dimensions.case: Iranian state-linked video ending with “One vengeance for all.”

dimensions.name: Synthetic Battlefield Representation
dimensions.description: Visualization of a threatened, imagined, or unverified battlefield outcome without waiting for physical evidence.

dimensions.name: Relational Fabrication
dimensions.description: Synthetic depiction of distinct actors as participating in a shared interaction or coordinated relationship not established by independent evidence.

key_findings: Generative AI is lowering the cost and increasing the speed and scale of wartime narrative production.
The U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict illustrates synthetic mobilization, synthetic battlefield representation, and relational fabrication as overlapping analytical functions.
Human attention is an incomplete measure of information availability in an environment mediated by search, retrieval, language models, and AI agents.
Machine addressability should not be confused with retrieval, acceptance, model incorporation, influence, or downstream action.
Narrative occupancy is an observable property of information persistence rather than evidence of persuasion or propaganda success.
Correction can improve epistemic accuracy if systems preserve negation, provenance, and source dependence, but can reinforce erroneous association if qualifiers are lost.
Synthetic artifacts should remain evidentially distinct from verified physical events, recoverable evidence, technical data, and reliable independent reporting.
Epistemic compression is a key risk when event, claim, depiction, simulation, allegation, denial, and verification collapse during derivative processing.
The current evidence does not demonstrate deliberate machine-targeted propaganda, agent-directed intent, or actual downstream machine retrieval in the examined cases.

Synthetic-content production should be tracked within MCCM as a provenance-rich input to existing narrative-amplification and information-distortion mechanisms rather than a new quantified indicator at this stage.
policy_recommendations: Complement reach, engagement, and sentiment monitoring with limited retrieval-oriented testing of machine-mediated visibility.
Preserve source attribution, evidentiary qualification, correction, negation, and source dependence when automated systems handle contested wartime claims.
Treat terms such as claimed, depicted, AI-generated, denied, and independently verified as substantive information rather than stylistic qualifiers.
Extend provenance practices beyond original media assets into screenshots, transcripts, quotations, news reports, and machine-generated summaries.
Test whether systems can identify derivative references that originate from a single synthetic artifact rather than treating repetition as independent corroboration.

Maintain a minimal monitoring record for synthetic-content tracking, including original artifact and publication date, claim/depicton/denial/verification status, original source and derivative lineage, retrieval date/system/query, and whether qualification was preserved in output.
Avoid treating machine accessibility as machine belief or measured influence without separate evidence of retrieval, incorporation, output generation, or downstream action.
